passage:
Jin spread a folder across the kitchen table in Rotterdam and started talking to nobody in particular, the way Jin did when a problem was too big to hold silently.
"Cover from the insurer, that's page two. What does it pay, and what does it leave? Savings, about a year of normal life. Employer, ten days of paid leave, and maybe more if I ask. And the public support scheme, which might cover transport to the hospital."
Jin wrote the four columns and phoned the hospital's billing office for a rough range of costs by month.
Astrid, Jin's sister, came in with tea and read the page. "You've made it smaller," Astrid said.
"No, just visible," Jin answered. "So money isn't one more surprise."

qa.q: Which city is the kitchen table in?
qa.a: The kitchen table is in Rotterdam.

qa.q: What was Jin feeling while sorting the folder into four columns?
qa.a: Jin was anxious about a problem that felt too big and wanted to make it manageable so that money would not add another surprise.

qa.q: What could Jin do if the billing office's range turns out too low?
qa.a: Jin could update the columns with the new figure and ask the employer and the scheme what else is available.

qa.q: How might Astrid have felt reading Jin's four columns?
qa.a: Astrid seemed relieved and impressed, saying that Jin had made the problem smaller, which suggests the page eased a shared worry.

grounding: The passage shows a person listing insurance, savings, employer support and public schemes, with a rough month-by-month cost, so that money does not add surprises.

subtype: Approach: avoiding the topic to stay hopeful [Pitfall]
passage:
I live next door to Dilnaz's family, so I saw what happened, and I still don't know what each person was really feeling. When Dilnaz's father got the news, the family made a rule: no one says the word. "It will pass," Dilnaz's mother told visitors. Whenever I asked how things were, Dilnaz smiled and changed the subject to the weather.
For months nobody sat down to ask what he wanted from his care, or how bills would be handled. Papers sat in a drawer.
Then one night the ambulance came. In the hospital corridor I watched the family sign forms in a rush, with no clue about his wishes. Dilnaz stood by the wall, very quiet.
— Nitin

qa.q: What was the rule the family made when the news came?
qa.a: The rule was that no one says the word.

qa.q: What might Dilnaz have been feeling when smiling and changing the subject?
qa.a: Dilnaz may have been frightened and holding on to hope, though Nitin cannot be sure, since the smile and quick change of subject could be protection.

qa.q: What could the family have done during the months before the emergency?
qa.a: They could have set aside a calm hour to ask the father what he wanted and to look at the papers together.

qa.q: What is it like for Nitin to watch the family in the corridor?
qa.a: Nitin felt helpless and sorry, watching people who cared deeply sign forms without knowing the father's wishes.

grounding: The account shows a family refusing to discuss how serious a diagnosis is, delaying talks on care and money until an emergency forces rushed decisions.

passage:
Subject: A plan so you can rest

Dear Devika,

Last night I saw you fall asleep at Amma's bedside with the phone in your hand. I have been thinking about it all day. For two months you have done every night and every visit, and I let it happen because you never complained. That was wrong of me.

One person cannot hold this up for the long run, so here is a plan. You take nights on Monday, Wednesday and Friday. I take the other nights and weekends. We hire a helper from ten to two on weekdays. And Thursday is your day off, no phone.

If it does not work, we change it. But please say yes.

Jasleen

qa.q: Which day is Devika's day off?
qa.a: Thursday is Devika's day off.

qa.q: How does Jasleen feel about the past two months?
qa.a: Jasleen feels guilty and worried, admitting that letting Devika carry everything was wrong.

qa.q: What could Jasleen and Devika do if the hired helper does not suit Amma?
qa.a: They could try a different helper or change the hours, and adjust the rest of the schedule so nobody is overloaded.

qa.q: How might Devika feel reading the email?
qa.a: Devika may feel relief at the offer of rest but also some reluctance to let go, since Devika has held the whole load for two months.

grounding: The email shows a person who realises one sibling cannot carry everything and plans rest shifts, paid help for some hours and a day off.

subtype: Approach: asking the patient about their wishes [Action]
passage:
On a mild Sunday evening the family gathered on the porch in Nairobi with Abebe, Esther's father, in the wide chair. Esther had rehearsed her question all week and still felt her throat tighten.
"Papa," she said softly, "we want to do this the way you would want. Would you like to hear every detail from the doctor, or would you like us to hear it first?"
Abebe thought for a while. "I want to hear everything myself," he said. "And I want to be home for as much as I can. Not too many calls to far-away relatives yet. Let me tell them when I am ready."
Esther wrote each wish in a small notebook, and read it back to him to be sure.

qa.q: Where did the family gather?
qa.a: The family gathered on the porch in Nairobi.

qa.q: What was Esther feeling as she asked her question?
qa.a: Esther was nervous and tender: she had rehearsed all week and her throat tightened.

qa.q: What could the family do if a later choice does not match Abebe's wishes?
qa.a: They could sit with Abebe again, show him the notebook and ask how he wants the new choice handled.

qa.q: How might Abebe have felt being asked instead of told?
qa.a: Abebe was probably respected and relieved to be asked, since Abebe answered with clear wishes without hesitating.

grounding: The passage shows a family gently asking a parent how to be treated and informed, so that plans follow the parent's own wishes.

subtype: Approach: revising the plan after treatment response [Revision]
passage:
It was exam week for the children, the monsoon had cut the road twice, and Madhav's father was tired and sick to his stomach after the first round of treatment. The plan on paper was not working.
On Tuesday Madhav and his wife Leela sat with the doctor. "We can adjust the timing and the plan," the doctor said. "Tell me what you're seeing at home." Leela had it written in a small diary.
That evening they redid the week. Madhav asked his manager to start later on treatment days. Leela swapped the school run with a neighbour. They also trimmed two spending items to cover the change.
Papa was quieter at supper, but ate more than he had in days.

qa.q: Who did Madhav and Leela meet on Tuesday?
qa.a: They met the doctor.

qa.q: What was Madhav probably feeling when he saw the first treatment plan was not working?
qa.a: Madhav was likely worried and guilty as he watched his father suffer, which is why he was quick to sit with the doctor.

qa.q: What could the family do if the second plan also causes problems?
qa.a: They could go back to the doctor with the diary notes and adjust again, rather than waiting or guessing at home.

qa.q: How might Leela have felt keeping the diary and reorganising the week?
qa.a: Leela probably felt stretched but purposeful, since the diary gave the doctor clear detail and made a hard week manageable.

grounding: The passage shows a family who, after side effects, talk to the doctor about changes, rework schedules at work and home, and adjust spending.

passage:
The hospital corridor hummed all night, and Mehak had slept badly for weeks, waiting for news about her father. On Thursday she dropped a cup twice and snapped at a nurse, then stood in the stairwell shaking with tiredness.
Her friend Simran found her there. "You're running on nothing," Simran said. "Please talk to the hospital counsellor. I'll sit with your father for an hour."
Mehak wanted to say she was fine. Instead she nodded.
The counsellor listened without hurrying, and they made a small plan: a short walk each day, a cousin on Saturday nights, and one friend to text. Mehak went back that evening feeling lighter, not fixed, and she was gentler with the nurse.

qa.q: What did Mehak drop twice on Thursday?
qa.a: Mehak dropped a cup twice.

qa.q: What was Mehak feeling in the stairwell?
qa.a: Mehak was exhausted and close to tears, and she nearly said she was fine before agreeing to get help.

qa.q: What could Mehak do if the small plan feels hard to keep?
qa.a: Mehak could ask Simran to walk with her or let the counsellor know and change the plan.

qa.q: How might Simran have felt finding Mehak in the stairwell?
qa.a: Simran was probably worried and caring, shown by speaking plainly and offering to sit with the father.

grounding: The passage shows a young adult who, after weeks of poor sleep, notices exhaustion and accepts a friend's suggestion to see a counsellor and take short breaks.

subtype: Approach: reviewing goals and time horizon [Thinking]
passage:
I'm Charu, and when the market fell by a fifth last spring, I felt sick opening my account. Everything I owned looked smaller.
My friend Himani asked one question: "When do you need this money?" Not "what should you do", just that.
I took a piece of paper and made two piles. One was my retirement savings, which I won't touch for decades. The other was the deposit for a flat, which I hoped to use in two years. They had sat side by side in my head as one number, and that was the problem.
The first pile could wait out the storm. The second one needed a proper look, maybe with a registered adviser. I still felt uneasy, but for the first time the fear had edges.
— Charu

qa.q: How long is the flat deposit meant to wait?
qa.a: The deposit is meant to wait two years.

qa.q: What was Charu feeling when opening the account?
qa.a: Charu felt sick and anxious as everything looked smaller, though the fear got edges once the two piles were separated.

qa.q: What could Charu do about the flat deposit?
qa.a: Charu could talk with a registered adviser to understand the general options for money needed within two years.

qa.q: Why might Himani have asked when the money is needed, instead of telling Charu what to do?
qa.a: Himani may have wanted Charu to see the answer through Charu's own goals, since the question itself made the difference.

grounding: The reflection shows a young investor asking when money is needed after a fall and treating decades-away savings differently from money needed within two years.

subtype: Approach: panic selling at the bottom [Pitfall]
passage:
The prices fell for eleven days in a row. In his small town, Francis checked the phone at the tea stall, at the bus stop, and at night under the blanket. Videos on the phone said everything would go to zero.
On the twelfth day, hands shaking, Francis sold every unit and felt the knot in the stomach loosen at once. "At least it stops," Francis told Saurabh, the shopkeeper next door, who had said "wait" a week earlier.
Three months later, prices were back up. Saurabh, who had kept his holdings and added nothing new, said only, "It came back." The paper loss Francis had feared was now a real one, and the calm from selling was gone.
Francis stared at the number for a long time.

qa.q: How many days in a row did the prices fall?
qa.a: The prices fell for eleven days in a row.

qa.q: What was Francis feeling when selling every unit?
qa.a: Francis was frightened and desperate to end the pain, and felt brief relief once the selling was done.

qa.q: What could Francis do differently if prices fall again?
qa.a: Francis could decide beforehand what would count as a reason to sell and check the news only on a fixed day.

qa.q: How might Saurabh have felt telling Francis "It came back"?
qa.a: Saurabh was probably sympathetic and did not want to gloat, given the plain, quiet remark.

grounding: The passage shows an investor who sells everything to stop the pain of daily losses, then watches prices recover without them so the loss becomes real.

passage:
The prices dropped the week Ritu's scooter needed a new part, and the bank's message about the monthly instalment arrived on the same morning. Hrithik, a colleague at the next desk, looked over. "Stop it for now. Wait till the bottom, then buy."
Ritu opened her notebook. On the first page, written before any fall: "Same amount, same date, every month. No guessing."
"I can't tell where the bottom is," Ritu said. "Nobody can. But if the price is low, the same money buys more units."
"And the scooter?"
"I'll cut something else for a month."
The instalment went through at ten, and Ritu turned back to work with her stomach still tight.

qa.q: What did Ritu's notebook say on its first page?
qa.a: The notebook said "Same amount, same date, every month. No guessing."

qa.q: What was Ritu feeling as the instalment went through?
qa.a: Ritu felt nervous, as the tight stomach shows, but she stuck to the rule she had set.

qa.q: What could Ritu do if money becomes too tight to keep the instalment?
qa.a: Ritu could write a new rule in the notebook to lower the amount for a month or two while calm, and raise it again later.

qa.q: How might Hrithik have seen Ritu's choice?
qa.a: Hrithik probably thought it risky and wanted to protect Ritu from more losses, which is why he said to stop it for now.

grounding: The passage shows an investor keeping a fixed monthly instalment through a fall, on a rule made beforehand, buying more units at lower prices without guessing the bottom.

subtype: Approach: checking the emergency fund first [Thinking]
passage:
I'm Francis. When the crash headlines came, I opened the investing page and my finger hovered over the button. Then I remembered Joseph.
Joseph was laid off last winter, in the middle of a fall, and had to sell his units at a bad price just to pay rent. He told me over tea that the loss was not the market's fault. It was that his cushion had been too thin.
So before doing anything, I sat with a notebook. My monthly costs come to 40,000, so six months is 2,40,000. I checked the balance in my savings accounts: 2,55,000, safe and easy to reach. I felt the knot in my chest ease.
Only after that did I look at the investing page again.
— Francis

qa.q: How much did Francis's savings accounts hold?
qa.a: The savings accounts held 2,55,000.

qa.q: What was Francis feeling before checking the balance?
qa.a: Francis was uneasy and hesitant, hovering over the button, and felt relief when the balance covered six months.

qa.q: What could Francis do if the balance had been lower than six months of costs?
qa.a: Francis could build the cushion first with a monthly saving and delay any new investment until it was there.

qa.q: What might Joseph want others to learn from what happened?
qa.a: Joseph may want others to see that a thin cushion forced a sale in a fall, which is why the story stuck with Francis.

grounding: The reflection shows a person confirming six months of expenses in safe accounts before an investment decision, so that a job loss would not force a sale at a loss.
